idiom_name: for await over AsyncSequence (AsyncStream continuation) / Combine publisher.sink
implementation_notes: Swift's platform is push-invoked by design: an AsyncStream is built from a closure that receives a continuation, and adapting a callback- or delegate-based client is exactly continuation.yield(...) in the client callback while the consumer coroutine is resumed per delivery - no thread while idle, as Apple's documentation presents it. Combine offers the closure form (publisher.sink(receiveValue:) returns an AnyCancellable that owns the subscription). A delegate object remains the right shape when the client API is delegate-based; wrap it in a stream so the stream owns start/stop lifecycle.
pitfalls: AsyncStream buffers without bound by default; choose a buffering policy (.bufferingNewest(n)/.bufferingOldest(n)) or a slow consumer grows memory.
Wire client shutdown to continuation.onTermination/finish, otherwise callbacks keep yielding into an abandoned stream and the client leaks.
An AsyncStream is single-consumer: two tasks iterating the same stream split the messages, so create one stream per consumer.
Combine sinks and continuation.yield run on the producer's scheduler; work that needs actor isolation must hop explicitly.
